section.title: Return to Bethel
section.sectionRationale: After the disaster at Shechem, God recalls Jacob to Bethel, the place of his first vision, to worship and to hear the covenant renewed. The chapter gathers threads of a lifetime: idols buried, the name Israel confirmed, Rachel's death, and the burial of Isaac.
section.thesis: God graciously brings His wandering servant home to worship, purifies his household of idols, confirms the covenant name and promises, and carries the family through birth and death toward the future He has sworn.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the call to purify and return to Bethel; the renewal of the name and covenant; the birth of Benjamin and the death of Rachel; and the twelve sons and the burial of Isaac.

verses.text: Then God said to Jacob, “Arise, go up to {{bethel|Bethel}}, and settle there. Build an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau.”
So Jacob told his household and all who were with him, “Get rid of the foreign gods that are among you. Purify yourselves and change your garments.
Then let us arise and go to Bethel. I will build an altar there to God, who answered me in my day of distress. He has been with me wherever I have gone.”
So they gave Jacob all their foreign gods and all their earrings, and Jacob buried them under the oak near Shechem.
As they set out, a terror from God fell over the surrounding cities, so that they did not pursue Jacob’s sons.
So Jacob and everyone with him arrived in Luz (that is, Bethel) in the land of Canaan.
There Jacob built an altar, and he called that place El-bethel, because it was there that God had revealed Himself to Jacob as he fled from his brother.
Now Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, died and was buried under the oak below Bethel. So Jacob named it Allon-bacuth.
After Jacob had returned from Paddan-aram, God appeared to him again and blessed him.
And God said to him, “Though your name is Jacob, you will no longer be called Jacob. Instead, your name will be {{israel|Israel}}.” So God named him Israel.
And God told him, “I am {{elshaddai|God Almighty}}. Be fruitful and multiply. A nation, even a company of nations, shall come from you, and kings shall descend from you.
The land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you, and I will give this land to your descendants after you.”
Then God went up from the place where He had spoken with him.
So Jacob set up a pillar in the place where God had spoken with him, a stone marker, and he poured out a drink offering on it and anointed it with oil.
Jacob called the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.

units.label: Benjamin born, Rachel dies
units.note: son of my sorrow, son of my right hand

verses.text: Later, they set out from Bethel, and while they were still some distance from Ephrath, Rachel began to give birth, and her labor was difficult.
During her severe labor, the midwife said to her, “Do not be afraid, for you are having another son.”
And with her last breath, for she was dying, she named him {{benoni|Ben-oni}}. But his father called him Benjamin.
So Rachel died and was buried on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem).
Jacob set up a pillar on her grave; it marks Rachel’s tomb to this day.

units.label: The twelve sons and Isaac's death
units.note: a family and a father gathered to his people

verses.text: Israel again set out and pitched his tent beyond the Tower of Eder.
While Israel was living in that region, Reuben went in and slept with his father’s concubine Bilhah, and Israel heard about it. Jacob had twelve sons:
The sons of Leah were Reuben the firstborn of Jacob, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun.
The sons of Rachel were Joseph and Benjamin.
The sons of Rachel’s maidservant Bilhah were Dan and Naphtali.
And the sons of Leah’s maidservant Zilpah were Gad and Asher. These are the sons of Jacob, who were born to him in Paddan-aram.
Jacob returned to his father Isaac at Mamre, near Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), where Abraham and Isaac had stayed.
And Isaac lived 180 years.
Then he breathed his last and died and was gathered to his people, old and full of years. And his sons Esau and Jacob buried him.

bethel.gloss: House of God. It is the place where Jacob first met God in a dream with a ladder to heaven, Genesis 28. God now calls him back there to worship, so the name marks both the beginning and the renewal of Jacob's walk with the Lord who keeps His promises.

israel.gloss: The name means he struggles with God or God strives. First given at Peniel, Genesis 32, it is confirmed here at Bethel. The grasping heel-holder Jacob is remade into Israel, and the name becomes the name of the whole covenant people through whom God will bless the nations.

elshaddai.gloss: God Almighty, the name by which God revealed Himself to Abraham when He gave the covenant of many descendants, Genesis 17. By using it here, God ties Jacob's blessing to the same sworn promise of nations, kings, and land that runs from Abraham to Christ.

benoni.gloss: Son of my sorrow, or possibly son of my strength, the name the dying Rachel gives her last son. Jacob renames him Benjamin, son of my right hand, turning a name of grief into one of favor and hope, a small picture of God bringing life and blessing out of sorrow.

basic.context: After the horror at Shechem, God calls Jacob to return to Bethel, the place where he first met God when fleeing Esau. Jacob purifies his household, buries their idols, and builds an altar. There God renews his new name, Israel, and the covenant promises before the family journeys on through Rachel's death and Isaac's burial.
basic.hermeneutics: The key question is why God calls Jacob back to Bethel now. The answer is grace: God recalls His wandering servant to worship and to hear the promise again after a season of compromise and violence. The chapter is about renewal and covenant faithfulness, not merely travel notes.
basic.originalLanguages: Bethel means house of God, the place of Jacob's first vision. His new name Israel means one who struggles with God. God identifies Himself as El-Shaddai, God Almighty, the covenant name from Abraham. And the dying Rachel names her son Ben-oni, son of my sorrow, which Jacob turns to Benjamin, son of my right hand.
basic.typology: The buried idols and changed garments picture the cleansing God's people need before worship, fulfilled in the washing Christ gives. Rachel dies near Bethlehem, and her weeping is later echoed in Matthew at the birth of Christ. The promise of kings from Jacob points to David and to King Jesus.
basic.christ: God swears again that kings will come from Jacob's body, a promise that runs through Judah to David and finally to Jesus, the King of kings. Rachel is buried on the way to Bethlehem, the town where the promised King would be born, quietly tying this chapter to the coming of Christ.
basic.god: God is the initiator here. He calls, He protects with a terror over the cities, He appears, He blesses, and He renews His promises. Even amid grief and death, God keeps moving His plan forward, showing Himself faithful to a family that has been anything but faithful.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 28 records Jacob's first meeting with God at Bethel. Jeremiah 31 hears Rachel weeping for her children. Matthew 2 applies that weeping to the slaughter near Bethlehem, tying Rachel's tomb to the coming of Christ.
basic.oneStory: This is a chapter of coming home. God gathers His servant back to worship, renews the covenant name and promises, and carries the family through birth and death toward the King who will one day be born near Rachel's grave in Bethlehem.

context.literary:
Genesis 35 closes the long account of Isaac's family that began at Genesis 25:19, and it does so by tying up threads from across Jacob's life. Its structure moves from worship to loss: a journey to Bethel and an altar, verses 1 to 8; a divine appearance and a renewed covenant, verses 9 to 15; a birth and a death on the road, verses 16 to 20; a sin, a list of sons, and a funeral, verses 21 to 29. Three deaths mark the chapter, Deborah, Rachel and Isaac, and each is marked by a burial place.

The opening scene answers Genesis 28 point by point. There Jacob fled from Esau and met God at Luz, set up a pillar, poured oil on it, named the place Bethel, and vowed that if God brought him back safely, 'then the LORD will be my God,' Genesis 28:20-22. Here God commands him to go back to Bethel, verse 1; Jacob builds an altar there to 'God, who answered me in my day of distress,' verse 3; he sets up a pillar and pours oil on it, verse 14; and he names the place Bethel again, verse 15. The vow is fulfilled and the story of Jacob's journey comes full circle.

God's speech in verses 10 to 12 gathers the language of earlier promises. The renaming repeats Genesis 32:28. 'I am God Almighty' repeats Genesis 17:1. 'Be fruitful and multiply' reaches back through Genesis 28:3 and Genesis 9:1 to Genesis 1:28. The promise of kings recalls Genesis 17:6. The chapter presents Jacob as the heir of the whole promise, creation blessing included.

The final section is compressed and list-like. Reuben's sin is told in half a verse, verse 22, and the narrative moves straight into the list of twelve sons, verses 22 to 26, as if the family must now be counted as the foundation of the nation. For the first time since the renaming the narrator himself calls Jacob 'Israel,' verses 21 and 22, then returns to 'Jacob' within the same verse, a pattern of alternation that continues through the rest of Genesis.

The chapter ends with Isaac's death, verse 29. Genesis habitually closes one generation's account before opening the next, and chapter 36 turns to Esau before chapter 37 begins the account of Jacob's family.
context.historical:
Bethel lay in the central hill country a short distance north of Jerusalem. Its earlier name was Luz, verse 6, as Genesis 28:19 had noted. In later Israel it became one of Jeroboam's two royal sanctuaries, where he set up a golden calf, 1 Kings 12:28-29. Hosea mocked it as Beth-aven, 'house of wickedness,' Hosea 4:15, and Amos warned, 'Bethel will come to nothing,' Amos 5:5. For Israelite hearers the memory of Jacob purging idols on the way to Bethel stood in sharp contrast with the idolatry that later filled it.

The 'foreign gods' of verse 2 had several possible sources. Rachel had stolen her father's household idols, Genesis 31:19, and the plunder of Shechem, Genesis 34:29, would have brought foreign objects and people into the camp. The earrings handed over with them, verse 4, were often associated with religious practices in the ancient world; Aaron made the golden calf from earrings, Exodus 32:2-4, and Gideon's ephod, which became a snare, was made from earrings taken as plunder, Judges 8:24-27. Burying them under the oak at Shechem put them permanently out of use.

Deborah, 'Rebekah's nurse,' verse 8, is named for the first time here. An unnamed nurse had travelled with Rebekah from Haran, Genesis 24:59. How she came to be with Jacob is not explained, but her death and the name 'oak of weeping' suggest she was a beloved member of the household.

Rachel died 'on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem),' verse 19. The parenthetical note identifies the place for later readers. Samuel later speaks of 'Rachel's tomb in Zelzah on the border of Benjamin,' 1 Samuel 10:2, which some take to point further north.

Isaac's death at 180, verse 28, is recorded here to close his story, but the numbers of Genesis place it later. Isaac was sixty at the twins' birth, Genesis 25:26, so Jacob was 120 at Isaac's death. Jacob was 130 when he met Pharaoh, Genesis 47:9, so Isaac died during Joseph's years in Egypt. The narrator closes Isaac's account before turning to Joseph, rather than following strict chronological order.
context.canonical:
This chapter is the turning point from Jacob's personal story to the story of the twelve tribes. The list in verses 22 to 26 is the first complete roster of Jacob's sons, and the twelve become the frame of Israel's life: twelve stones on the high priest's breastpiece, Exodus 28:21, twelve tribes of the land allotment in Joshua, and in the end 'twelve gates inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel,' Revelation 21:12.

Bethel becomes a byword for meeting God. Hosea recalls that Jacob 'found Him at Bethel and spoke with Him there,' Hosea 12:4, and the call to 'Get rid of the foreign gods that are among you,' verse 2, is echoed almost exactly when Joshua renews the covenant at Shechem: 'get rid of the foreign gods among you and incline your hearts to the LORD,' Joshua 24:23. Samuel says the same to Israel: 'rid yourselves of the foreign gods,' 1 Samuel 7:3. Returning to God in Israel's history always involved putting away idols.

The promise of kings, verse 11, is traced through Judah, Genesis 49:10, to David, and then to Jesus, whom the angel promised would 'reign over the house of Jacob forever,' Luke 1:33.

Rachel's death near Bethlehem is taken up twice. The women of Bethlehem bless Ruth, 'May the LORD make the woman entering your home like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel,' Ruth 4:11. Jeremiah hears 'Rachel weeping for her children,' Jeremiah 31:15, as the exiles pass on their way to Babylon, and Matthew applies the verse to Herod's slaughter of the boys of Bethlehem, Matthew 2:17-18.

Benjamin's line matters later. Israel's first king, Saul, was a Benjamite, 1 Samuel 9:1-2, and so was the apostle Paul, 'of the tribe of Benjamin,' Philippians 3:5. Reuben's sin, verse 22, costs him the birthright, which Genesis 49:3-4 and 1 Chronicles 5:1-2 explain. The Tower of Eder, verse 21, means tower of the flock, and Micah 4:8 addresses Jerusalem as 'O watchtower of the flock,' promising that 'the former dominion will be restored to you.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to understand that worship requires cleansing. The first thing Jacob does when God calls him to Bethel is to deal with the idols in his household, verse 2. Israel, who would later be told to destroy the idols of Canaan, Deuteronomy 7:5, and who would struggle with foreign gods for centuries, needed to see that its father had to purge his own camp before he could meet God.

He also wanted Israel to see that God's promises are anchored in God, not in the family's performance. After the moral chaos of chapter 34, the chapter opens with God speaking, verse 1, protecting, verse 5, appearing, verse 9, naming, verse 10, and promising, verses 11 and 12. Israel was a nation because of what God had said to Jacob at Bethel, and the chapter repeats those words so that later generations would know them.

Finally, Moses wanted Israel to see that the promise moves forward through sorrow. The chapter records the deaths of three people Jacob loved and the betrayal of his firstborn. Blessing and grief are placed side by side. Israel would face exile, loss and bereavement, and this chapter taught them that God's word stands even at a graveside.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Jacob's household ritual, removing idols, purifying themselves and changing clothes, is described, not commanded as a permanent rite. Israel later received specific laws of purification, but the principle here is broader: meeting God requires turning from other gods.

The pillar, the drink offering and the oil, verse 14, are patriarchal acts of worship that predate the tabernacle. They are not a pattern for Christian worship, and later law forbade setting up sacred pillars, Deuteronomy 16:22, because of their association with Canaanite religion. The chapter records them as what was fitting in Jacob's day.

Reuben's sin, verse 22, is recorded without comment, but it is not approved. Its consequence appears in Genesis 49:4. The brevity of the report should not be read as indifference.

What carries forward is the call to consecration and the comfort of God's promises. Paul applies the same logic: 'since we have these promises, let us cleanse ourselves from everything that defiles body and spirit,' 2 Corinthians 7:1. And John's last word to the church could be Jacob's word to his household: 'Little children, keep yourselves from idols,' 1 John 5:21.

debates.question: Is the naming of Israel here a new event or a confirmation of the name given at Peniel in Genesis 32?

views.label: A solemn confirmation
views.case: The name was first given at Peniel, Genesis 32:28; here at Bethel God formally reaffirms it in a covenant setting, sealing what was declared before and tying it to the El-Shaddai promises. The pattern of Abraham's renaming, Genesis 17:5, joined to the El-Shaddai speech, supports this.

views.label: A second, distinct bestowal
views.case: Some read the repetition as a fresh act at a new location, underscoring that the transformation is now complete and publicly established as Jacob returns in obedience. Others see two traditions of the renaming placed side by side.

debates.bearing: Either way, the point stands: God fixes the new identity of Israel at the place of worship, grounding the covenant people's name in His initiative and grace rather than in Jacob's striving.

debates.question: Why did Reuben sleep with Bilhah?

views.label: A bid for leadership
views.case: In the ancient world taking a ruler's concubine was a claim to his authority. Absalom slept with David's concubines to show he had displaced his father, 2 Samuel 16:21-22, and Solomon took Adonijah's request for Abishag as a request for the kingdom, 1 Kings 2:22. With Rachel dead, Reuben may have been asserting himself as heir and preventing Bilhah, Rachel's maid, from replacing his mother Leah's rival.

views.label: Lust and disregard
views.case: The text gives no motive, and Jacob's later verdict speaks of Reuben as 'Uncontrolled as the waters,' Genesis 49:4, suggesting unrestrained passion rather than calculation.

debates.bearing: Whatever the motive, the result is the same: Reuben loses the birthright, 1 Chronicles 5:1. The political reading helps explain why the event is placed right after Rachel's death and why its consequences are so severe.

debates.question: Where was Rachel buried?

views.label: Near Bethlehem in Judah
views.case: Genesis 35:19 and Genesis 48:7 both say 'on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem),' and Ruth 4:11 connects Rachel with Bethlehem. The traditional site of Rachel's tomb lies just north of Bethlehem.

views.label: Further north, on the border of Benjamin
views.case: 1 Samuel 10:2 places Rachel's tomb 'in Zelzah on the border of Benjamin,' and Jeremiah 31:15 hears her weeping in Ramah, north of Jerusalem. Some suggest the Ephrath in view was a different place and the Bethlehem note identifies it with the better known town.

debates.bearing: The texts may reflect a region rather than a precise spot. What matters theologically is that Scripture ties Rachel's grief to both Benjamin and Bethlehem, and Matthew draws both together at the birth of Jesus.

study.originalLanguages:
The basic study explains Bethel, Israel, El-Shaddai and the two names of Benjamin. Several more words and constructions shape the chapter.

The 'foreign gods' of verses 2 and 4 are elohei hannekar, literally 'gods of the foreigner.' The command 'Get rid of' uses the causative of sur, to turn aside or remove. The whole phrase, 'Get rid of the foreign gods that are among you,' reappears almost word for word in Joshua 24:23 and in 1 Samuel 7:3. It became a fixed call to covenant renewal in Israel. 'Purify yourselves' is the reflexive form of taher, the word that later governs ritual cleanness in Leviticus.

Verse 5 speaks of 'a terror from God.' The noun comes from the root chatat, to be shattered or dismayed, the verb Moses uses when he says, 'Do not be afraid or discouraged,' Deuteronomy 1:21. The same God who tells His people not to be shattered brings shattering fear on their enemies.

Verse 7 contains a grammatical oddity. 'God had revealed Himself' translates a plural verb with Elohim as subject. Normally, when Elohim refers to the true God, its verbs are singular. Some explain the plural as agreement with the plural form of the noun, others as a reference to God together with the angels Jacob saw at Bethel, Genesis 28:12. The verb itself, galah, to uncover or reveal, is a key word of revelation.

In verse 11 God promises 'a company of nations.' The noun is qahal, an assembly or congregation, the word later used for 'the whole assembly of Israel,' Deuteronomy 31:30. Isaac had prayed that Jacob would become 'a company of peoples,' Genesis 28:3, and Jacob recalls God's word as 'a multitude of peoples,' Genesis 48:4. 'Kings shall descend from you' is literally 'kings shall come out from your loins,' the language used of physical descent.

Verse 14 records the first drink offering in Scripture. The noun nesek and the verb nasak, to pour out, name an offering that later accompanies the daily sacrifices, Exodus 29:40. Paul uses the image of himself: 'I am being poured out like a drink offering,' Philippians 2:17.

In verse 18 the BSB's 'with her last breath' is literally 'as her soul was going out,' using nephesh, the life or self. The name Ben-oni is ambiguous, as the footnote says: the noun on can mean sorrow or strength. Jacob uses the same word of Reuben in Genesis 49:3, 'the beginning of my strength.' Rachel may have been naming her son for her grief, or for her last strength. Jacob's renaming to Benjamin, 'son of my right hand,' removes the ambiguity. Since yamin can also mean south, some hear a further note in the name as well: Benjamin was the only one of the twelve born in Canaan.

The Tower of Eder in verse 21 is migdal eder, 'tower of the flock,' the same phrase Micah uses for Jerusalem in Micah 4:8. Finally, verse 22 is unusual in the traditional Hebrew text, which places a section break in the middle of the verse after 'Israel heard about it.' The Greek Septuagint adds a phrase saying that it seemed evil to him. The Hebrew leaves Jacob's reaction unspoken until Genesis 49:4.

typology.type: Purging idols and changing garments before meeting God, Genesis 35:2
typology.fulfillment: Jacob's household buries its foreign gods, purifies itself and changes clothes before approaching the God of Bethel. The pattern recurs at Sinai, Exodus 19:10, and in every covenant renewal, Joshua 24:23. In Christ the cleansing goes deeper than garments. Believers draw near 'having our hearts sprinkled to cleanse us from a guilty conscience and our bodies washed with pure water,' Hebrews 10:22, and are told to put off the old self and put on the new, Ephesians 4:22-24. The type falls short because Jacob's household needed to be told again and again; the gospel gives a new heart that wants to be rid of idols.

typology.type: Ben-oni renamed Benjamin: the son of sorrow becomes the son of the right hand
typology.fulfillment: Rachel names her son out of her death pangs; Jacob gives him a name of honour and strength. The New Testament does not draw this line explicitly, so it is a pattern rather than a declared type, but it matches the shape of Christ's work. The Servant was 'a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief,' Isaiah 53:3, and was then 'exalted... to the right hand of God,' Acts 2:33. The escalation is that Benjamin's names described two views of one birth, while Christ truly passed through sorrow to the throne. The type falls short because Benjamin's sorrow was his mother's, while Christ's sorrow was His own, borne for others.

God promises Jacob a royal line, as He had promised Abraham, Genesis 17:6. The promise narrows through Judah, Genesis 49:10, to David, and then to Jesus, who was 'a descendant of David according to the flesh,' Romans 1:3. The angel told Mary He would 'reign over the house of Jacob forever,' Luke 1:33. The escalation is that the kings of Israel ruled a small nation for a time and often failed, while Christ is 'Lord of lords and King of kings,' Revelation 17:14. The type falls short because every other king from Jacob's body died; this King reigns forever.

typology.type: The pillar anointed and the drink offering poured, Genesis 35:14
typology.fulfillment: Jacob marks the place where God spoke with a stone, oil and a poured offering. The drink offering later accompanied Israel's daily sacrifices, Exodus 29:40, and Isaiah says the Servant 'poured out His life unto death,' Isaiah 53:12. Christ's self-giving is the reality to which every poured offering points. Paul then sees his own life as a drink offering poured on the sacrifice of the church's faith, Philippians 2:17. The type falls short because Jacob's offering soaked into a stone and was gone, while Christ's life poured out purchases eternal life, and those in Him become living stones, 1 Peter 2:5.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the promise of kings. God tells Jacob that 'kings shall descend from you,' verse 11. The rest of Genesis narrows that promise to Judah, Genesis 49:10, and the rest of the Old Testament narrows it further to David. Matthew's genealogy runs straight through this chapter, 'Isaac the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Judah and his brothers,' Matthew 1:2, and reaches 'David the king,' Matthew 1:6, and then Jesus. The angel's words to Mary, 'He will reign over the house of Jacob forever,' Luke 1:33, name the very man to whom this promise was spoken.

It leads to Christ through Bethlehem. Rachel dies and is buried on the road to Bethlehem, verse 19. Micah later foretells that out of 'Bethlehem Ephrathah' will come 'One to be ruler over Israel... whose origins are of old,' Micah 5:2. The same town that marks Rachel's grief becomes the birthplace of the King. Matthew connects the two when he applies Jeremiah's 'Rachel weeping for her children' to the grief of Bethlehem's mothers after Jesus' birth, Matthew 2:18. Rachel's sorrow in this chapter is taken up into the sorrow that surrounded the coming of Christ, and Jeremiah's next words promise comfort, Jeremiah 31:16-17.

It leads to Christ through the shape of Benjamin's two names. A son born in sorrow receives a name of honour at his father's right hand. The New Testament does not make this link itself, so it must be held lightly, but it fits the gospel pattern: the Son who was 'a man of sorrows,' Isaiah 53:3, is the one who 'sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high,' Hebrews 1:3.

It leads to Christ through the call to worship. Jacob's household purifies itself to meet God at Bethel, the house of God. Jesus presents Himself as the true Bethel, where the angels of God ascend and descend on the Son of Man, John 1:51. Believers no longer travel to a place to meet God; they come to Christ, and in Him they are being built into 'a spiritual house,' 1 Peter 2:5.

It leads to Christ through the twelve sons. The chapter lists the twelve who become the tribes of Israel. Jesus chose twelve apostles, and He promised they would sit 'on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel,' Matthew 19:28. The new Jerusalem bears the names of both, the tribes on its gates and the apostles on its foundations, Revelation 21:12-14.

Finally, the chapter's graves point to Christ by contrast. Deborah, Rachel and Isaac are buried, and pillars and trees mark their resting places. God is still the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and Jesus drew from that title the certainty of resurrection: 'He is not the God of the dead, but of the living,' Matthew 22:32.
study.god:
This chapter is full of God's initiative. He speaks first, verse 1. He protects the family with terror on the cities, verse 5. He appears again, verse 9. He blesses, names and promises, verses 9 to 12. And He goes up from the place where He spoke, verse 13, as He had gone up from Abraham, Genesis 17:22. The chapter presents a God who acts before His people respond, and who keeps coming back to a family that has repeatedly failed Him.

He is the God who answers in distress. Jacob calls Him the God 'who answered me in my day of distress,' verse 3. The word for distress echoes Genesis 32:7, where Jacob was 'in great fear and distress.' Jacob's theology has been formed by experience: God is the one who heard him when he was afraid. And He has been with him 'wherever I have gone,' verse 3, which fulfils the Bethel promise, 'I will watch over you wherever you go,' Genesis 28:15.

He is God Almighty, El-Shaddai. The title appears at key moments of promise in Genesis: to Abraham, Genesis 17:1; in Isaac's blessing, Genesis 28:3; here; and in Jacob's prayer for his sons, Genesis 43:14. God later tells Moses, 'I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob as God Almighty,' Exodus 6:3. The name stresses God's power to fulfil His word when human resources fail. Jacob's household is small, surrounded by enemies and grieving, but the Almighty promises nations and kings.

He is a jealous God who will not share His people's worship. The first act of preparation is to put away foreign gods, verse 2. God does not demand this in so many words, but Jacob understands that the God of Bethel cannot be approached by a household carrying other gods. The same God later says, 'You shall have no other gods before Me,' Exodus 20:3.

He is the God of the living through the deaths of His people. Deborah, Rachel and Isaac all die in this chapter. God does not prevent those deaths, and the chapter does not explain them. But the covenant promises are spoken between the burials, verses 9 to 12, and they are promises about descendants and land that none of those who die will see. God's faithfulness spans generations.

He is patient with a flawed family. The chapter includes Reuben's sin, verse 22, and yet the list of twelve sons follows immediately. God's purposes do not wait for His people to be worthy.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to come to God by putting away what competes with Him, to remember how He has answered us in distress, and to trust the Almighty at the graveside.

crossReferences.note: At Bethel Jacob set up a pillar, poured oil on it and vowed that if God brought him back safely, 'the LORD will be my God.' Genesis 35:1-15 is the fulfilment of that vow: Jacob returns, builds an altar, sets up a pillar, pours oil and a drink offering, and names the place Bethel again.

God had introduced Himself to Jacob in Haran as 'the God of Bethel, where you anointed the pillar and made a solemn vow to Me.' The command of Genesis 35:1 to go up to Bethel is God reminding Jacob of the vow he had not yet kept after settling at Shechem.

At Shechem Joshua tells Israel to 'get rid of the foreign gods among you and incline your hearts to the LORD.' It is nearly the same command Jacob gave his household in Genesis 35:2, also at Shechem, and it shows that covenant renewal always required putting away idols.

God appeared to Abram as 'God Almighty,' renamed him, and promised that 'kings will descend from you.' Genesis 35:10-12 follows the same pattern for Jacob: El-Shaddai appears, confirms a new name and promises kings, fruitfulness and land.

Near the end of his life Jacob tells Joseph, 'God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan, and there He blessed me.' He quotes the promise of Genesis 35:11-12 as the foundation for adopting Ephraim and Manasseh, showing how central this Bethel appearance was to him.

Jacob recalls with grief that 'Rachel died along the way in the land of Canaan, some distance from Ephrath.' Decades later the memory of Genesis 35:19 still shapes his words to Joseph, Rachel's firstborn.

'Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted.' Jeremiah pictures the mother who died in childbirth in Genesis 35:18 mourning her descendants carried into exile, and the following verses promise that they will return.

Matthew applies Jeremiah 31:15 to Herod's slaughter of Bethlehem's infants. Rachel's grave on the road to Bethlehem, Genesis 35:19, becomes a symbol of the grief that surrounded the birth of the promised King.

'But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah... out of you will come forth for Me One to be ruler over Israel.' The town named in Genesis 35:19 as the place of Rachel's burial becomes the birthplace of the King promised to Jacob in Genesis 35:11.

Jacob tells Reuben, 'you will no longer excel, because you went up to your father's bed.' The half verse of Genesis 35:22 receives its verdict here, and 1 Chronicles 5:1 adds that the birthright passed to Joseph's sons.

'Since we have these promises, let us cleanse ourselves from everything that defiles body and spirit.' Paul applies the same logic as Genesis 35: God's promises call His people to put away what defiles, as Jacob's household did before worship at Bethel.
The new Jerusalem has 'twelve gates inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel.' The twelve sons listed in Genesis 35:23-26 become the permanent frame of the city of God.

study.oneStory:
In the story of Scripture, Bethel is where heaven touched earth. Jacob's first night there, Genesis 28, showed a ladder between heaven and earth and a God who promised to be with a fugitive. His return in Genesis 35 shows that God kept the promise. The fall had driven humanity out of God's presence, Genesis 3:24. At Bethel God began to give His presence back to one family, at one place, as a pledge of what He would do for the world.

The chapter also shows the cost of living in a fallen world. The promise of fruitfulness, 'Be fruitful and multiply,' verse 11, echoes the creation blessing of Genesis 1:28. Yet within a few verses Rachel dies giving birth, verse 18. The pain in childbirth announced in Genesis 3:16 takes its toll even on the covenant family. Blessing and curse are woven together in the same chapter.

The chapter sets up what follows. The twelve sons listed here become the twelve tribes. The next chapters show those sons in conflict, sin and eventual reconciliation, and the book ends with them in Egypt, still carrying the promise of the land. The kings promised in verse 11 appear centuries later, and the house of God at Bethel gives way to the tabernacle and then the temple in Jerusalem.

The whole story moves toward Christ, in whom the promises of this chapter are fulfilled. He is the King descended from Jacob, born in Bethlehem near Rachel's grave. He is the true house of God, the place where heaven meets earth, John 1:51. He is the one through whom the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles become one people, and in whom the drink offering and the pillar find their meaning. He calls His people, as Jacob called his household, to put away idols and draw near.

The story ends in the new creation, where the chapter's themes reach their completion. The city of God bears the names of the twelve tribes on its gates, Revelation 21:12. God's dwelling is with humanity, Revelation 21:3, so there is no need to travel to Bethel. And there will be 'no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4. Rachel's death in childbirth, the oak of weeping, and Isaac's burial are answered by a world where no one needs a pillar to mark a grave.

quiz.q: Why does God call Jacob back to Bethel in this chapter?

options.text: To worship and renew the covenant at the place of his first vision, after failure.
options.note: Bethel was where God first met him; God graciously recalls him to worship.

options.text: To punish him for the slaughter at Shechem.
options.note: The move follows Shechem, but the call is one of grace and renewal, not punishment.

options.text: To give him a new plot of farmland.
options.note: The chapter is about worship and covenant, not land acquisition.

options.text: To hide him permanently from Esau.
options.note: Esau was already reconciled to Jacob in Genesis 33.

quiz.q: What did Jacob require of his household before going up to Bethel?

options.text: To put away foreign gods, purify themselves, and change their garments.
options.note: A decisive break with idols before worship, verses 2 to 4.

options.text: To gather more livestock for the journey.
options.note: They did travel with flocks, but the stated requirement was spiritual purification.

options.text: To swear vengeance on the Canaanites.
options.note: The chapter turns away from violence toward worship.

options.text: To build their own private altars first.
options.note: The altar was to be built to God at Bethel, not private shrines.

quiz.q: What promise does God renew to Jacob at Bethel?

options.text: That a company of nations and kings would come from him, with the land.
options.note: The El-Shaddai promise of nations, kings, and land, verses 11 to 12.

options.text: That he would never again face sorrow or loss.
options.note: In fact Rachel dies in the same chapter; the promise is covenantal, not a life free of grief.

options.text: That Joseph alone would inherit everything.
options.note: The promise concerns the whole people; Joseph's story unfolds later.

options.text: That Esau would serve him forever.
options.note: The renewed promise is about nations and kings, not dominance over Esau.

quiz.q: How does Rachel's death connect to the larger story of the Bible?

options.text: She is buried near Bethlehem, the town where the promised King would be born.
options.note: Her tomb and weeping tie to Bethlehem and are echoed in Matthew 2.

options.text: It proves God had rejected Jacob's family.
options.note: God is faithful throughout; grief does not signal rejection.

options.text: It marks the end of the covenant line.
options.note: The line continues; twelve sons are named in the same chapter.

options.text: It has no bearing on the rest of Scripture.
options.note: Jeremiah and Matthew both draw on Rachel's tomb and weeping.

quiz.q: What is the significance of the two names given to Rachel's last son?

options.text: Ben-oni, son of sorrow, is turned by Jacob into Benjamin, son of the right hand.
options.note: A father's hope spoken over a mother's grief, verse 18.

options.text: Both names mean the same thing and are interchangeable.
options.note: They are related but contrast sorrow with favor and strength.

options.text: The son was renamed to erase Rachel's memory.
options.note: The renaming honors hope, not erasure; Rachel's tomb is marked with a pillar.

options.text: The names refer to two different sons.
options.note: Both names belong to the one son born as Rachel dies.

questions: God called Jacob to bury the idols before worship. What foreign gods, the little securities you cling to, might God be calling you to put away?
Bethel was a place of return, where Jacob met God again after years of wandering. Is there a place, a promise, or a season of faith God is calling you to revisit?
God renewed His promise in the same chapter that Rachel died. How do you hold onto God's faithfulness when grief and blessing come mixed together?
Jacob turned Ben-oni, son of sorrow, into Benjamin, son of my right hand. Where might God be inviting you to name hope over a hard situation?
The promise of a coming King runs quietly through this chapter toward Bethlehem. How does knowing where the story is heading steady you in the ordinary births and deaths of your own life?

translationNotes.note: Ben-oni can mean son of my sorrow or son of my strength; Jacob's chosen name Benjamin means son of my right hand, deliberately turning grief toward favor.
God Almighty renders the Hebrew El-Shaddai, the covenant name used with Abraham in Genesis 17, linking Jacob's blessing to the same sworn promise.
The report of Reuben's sin is stated briefly and left without comment here, but it costs him the firstborn's blessing later in Genesis 49:3-4.
